props.title: Yes, Madam!
props.initialSlug: Two deadly women. One crazy ride.

sections.content: Yes, Madam! (1985) revolutionized Hong Kong action cinema by introducing "girls with guns" as a viable subgenre. Michelle Yeoh's film debut alongside Cynthia Rothrock created an explosive template that influenced decades of HK action. Director Corey Yuen's innovative fusion of hard-hitting martial arts, gunplay, and acrobatic stunts established a new style that would influence films like In the Line of Duty (1986) and Royal Warriors (1986). The film's success proved female-led action could draw massive audiences, paving the way for stars like Moon Lee and Joyce Godenzi.

sections.content: The mid-1980s marked a crucial turning point for Hong Kong action cinema. While Police Story (1985) showcased Jackie Chan's comedy-action innovation, Yes, Madam! demonstrated that serious female-driven action could be just as compelling. The film's influence extended beyond Asia - Cynthia Rothrock became America's first female martial arts star, while Michelle Yeoh's intense physical performance set a new standard that she'd later bring to Hollywood in films like Tomorrow Never Dies (1997) and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).

The technical innovations in Yes, Madam! can't be overstated. Corey Yuen's direction emphasized wide shots and long takes to showcase the authentic martial arts abilities of his leads. The finale's glass-filled office battle became instantly iconic, inspiring similar sequences in everything from Police Story (1985) to Hard Boiled (1992). The film's success also helped establish D&B Films as a major player in Hong Kong cinema, leading to more female-driven action productions. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: The ripple effects of Yes, Madam! continue today. Michelle Yeoh's recent Oscar win for Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) can be traced back to her groundbreaking debut. The film established a template for female action stars that influenced Western films like La Femme Nikita (1990) and Point of No Return (1993). Even modern movies like Atomic Blonde (2017) owe a debt to the hard-hitting style pioneered by Yeoh and Rothrock.
